# CorX Labs — complete site content

Source: https://corx-labs.com/
Last updated: 2026-08-01
Licence of described models: Apache 2.0

===============================================================================
SUMMARY
===============================================================================

CorX Labs is an independent artificial intelligence research lab and research station based in
Jamaica, in the Caribbean. It designs, trains and open-sources language models built from the
ground up: the architecture, the tokenizer, the data pipeline and the training loop are all written
in house. It does not fine-tune existing base models.

Slogan: "Architecting the future." Positioning: "from the ground up."
Founder: Nathan, a solo developer and independent AI researcher from Jamaica.
Contact: lkk89002@gmail.com
Website: https://corx-labs.com/
First and current release: CorX1.5 — https://huggingface.co/Sigmandndnns/CorX1.5-160M

===============================================================================
CORX1.5 — MODEL CARD
===============================================================================

CorX1.5 is an open-source language model with approximately 158 million parameters (157.8M), built
entirely from scratch by a single developer. Architecture, tokenizer, pretraining pipeline and
fine-tuning were all written and trained solo, on a single GPU, from the ground up. It is not a
fine-tune of an existing base model.

Hugging Face repository: Sigmandndnns/CorX1.5-160M
Developer: Nathan
Origin: Jamaica
Licence: Apache 2.0
Task: text generation
Status: actively trained; new data added on an ongoing basis

## Architecture

A custom decoder-only transformer, not copied from an existing model family.

- Positional encoding: RoPE — relative position information that extrapolates cleanly across the
  context window.
- Feed-forward: SwiGLU — gated activation, better quality per parameter than a plain MLP.
- Normalisation: RMSNorm — cheaper and more stable than LayerNorm at this scale.
- Role embeddings: a learned signal marking every token as user, assistant or raw text, so the
  model always knows whose turn it is. Most models infer this only from special tokens.
- Loss masking: assistant-only. The model is trained to predict only the tokens it should generate,
  not the user's side of the conversation.
- Parameters: 157.8M
- Layers: 10
- Context length: 1,024 tokens
- Vocabulary: 32,768-token custom BPE, trained for this model rather than reused

## Training pipeline

1. Pretraining — approximately 3 billion tokens across 25 open datasets spanning code, math,
   reasoning, conversation and general web text, with a held-out validation split and early
   stopping to catch overfitting.
2. Distillation — fine-tuned on responses generated by a larger teacher model (Qwen2.5-Instruct),
   with automated quality filtering that keeps only well-formatted, non-repetitive,
   correctly-verified answers.
3. Reasoning training — trained to show step-by-step work inside <think>...</think> blocks before
   answering, including verified worked arithmetic and debugging exercises containing a known,
   injected bug that the answer can be checked against.
4. Ongoing additions — new topics and targeted fixes are added continuously as gaps turn up in
   testing. Updated checkpoints are pushed to the Hugging Face repository; its commit history is the
   source of truth for what is current.

## What CorX1.5 is good at

- Holding a consistent identity and conversational style
- Short, direct answers to greetings and common everyday questions
- Declining requests it genuinely cannot fulfil — no internet access, no memory between chats, no
  tool access — instead of fabricating an answer
- Small worked arithmetic, shown step by step
- Recognising and explaining common Python bugs in a structured format

## What CorX1.5 is not

CorX1.5 was trained on a small fraction of the data used by comparable open models. Models in a
similar parameter range from major labs are typically trained on trillions of tokens; CorX1.5 was
trained on billions. It should not be relied on for:

- Broad factual knowledge or general reasoning outside its training patterns
- Complex or multi-step mathematics beyond basic arithmetic
- Production or safety-critical use of any kind

This is an independent research and learning project, not a competitor to frontier or lab-scale
models. It is shared in that spirit — small, transparent, and built to understand every part of how
it works.

## Safety

CorX1.5 includes a hardcoded response layer for messages indicating self-harm or crisis, which
returns a fixed set of crisis resources rather than a generated response. This is implemented in
code, not left to the model's judgment.

## Usage

CorX1.5 uses a custom architecture and is NOT compatible with AutoModel.from_pretrained() out of
the box. Load it with the model definition included in the repository (modeling_corx.py or the
provided inference script) alongside the checkpoint and tokenizer files.

    git lfs install
    git clone https://huggingface.co/Sigmandndnns/CorX1.5-160M
    cd CorX1.5-160M
    python inference.py

## Licence

Apache 2.0. Use, modification and redistribution are permitted, including commercially, provided
attribution and the licence notice are kept.

===============================================================================
ABOUT CORX LABS
===============================================================================

CorX Labs was founded by Nathan, a solo developer from Jamaica. For years the goal was the same:
build an AI — not adapt someone else's, but write the thing himself and train it from random
weights.

It started with APIs — an early chatbot built on top of Gemini and customised piece by piece, which
worked, but was never the same as building from the ground up. Then came fine-tuning, which failed:
slow GPUs, training runs that took far too long, and eventually the decision to walk away from that
approach.

CorX1.5 is what came out the other side: a custom transformer architecture, a tokenizer trained
from scratch, and a three-stage pipeline covering pretraining, distillation and reasoning —
designed, debugged and trained solo on a single GPU. Every checkpoint in the repository represents
real hours spent fixing data pipelines, chasing down overfitting, and learning how these systems
actually work underneath. It is open-sourced so other people can take it apart the same way.

## What CorX Labs stands for

- From the ground up. If we ship it, we wrote it. Understanding every part of a system is the point
  of building it, not a side effect.
- No overclaiming. A 158M-parameter model is a 158M-parameter model. The limits are documented as
  carefully as the capabilities.
- Open by default. Apache 2.0, published on Hugging Face, documented on corx-labs.com.

===============================================================================
DEVELOPERS
===============================================================================

CorX Labs is a one-person research lab.

Nathan — Founder and AI Researcher. A 14-year-old developer from Jamaica. He designed the
architecture, trained the tokenizer, wrote the pretraining and fine-tuning pipelines, curated the
data and ran every training job, solo, on a single GPU, from random weights. There is no team
behind CorX1.5 and no base model underneath it.

Journey:
- Age 12 — built a chatbot on top of Gemini's API and customised its behaviour. Useful, but it was
  somebody else's model wearing his configuration.
- Age 13 — moved to fine-tuning existing base models. It failed: slow GPUs, training runs that took
  far too long, and eventually he stopped.
- Age 14 — wrote a model instead of adapting one. Custom decoder-only transformer, tokenizer
  trained from scratch, ~3 billion tokens of pretraining across 25 open datasets, then distillation
  and reasoning training. The result is CorX1.5.
- Now — CorX1.5 is open-sourced under Apache 2.0 and still being trained, with updated checkpoints
  released as new data is added.

Contact: lkk89002@gmail.com

===============================================================================
BLOG: 3 BILLION TOKENS ON ONE GPU (2026-08-01)
===============================================================================

URL: https://corx-labs.com/blog/3-billion-tokens-one-gpu/
Author: Nathan

Core claim: 3 billion training tokens never need to fit in GPU memory. Tokens stream through the
GPU a batch at a time and are discarded. What has to fit is the model weights, their gradients, the
optimiser state, and the activations for one micro-batch — a couple of gigabytes for a 158M model,
and that figure does not change with dataset size. Dataset size is a disk and wall-clock problem;
model size is the memory problem.

Memory arithmetic for 157.8M parameters:
- Weights fp32: 4 bytes/param = 0.63 GB
- Gradients fp32: 4 bytes/param = 0.63 GB
- Adam first and second moments fp32: 8 bytes/param = 1.26 GB
- Subtotal: 16 bytes/param = 2.52 GB
- With 8-bit Adam moments (2 bytes/param instead of 8): 10 bytes/param = 1.58 GB
Activation memory sits on top of this and scales with batch size and sequence length.

The data pipeline: the corpus is tokenised once, offline, into a single flat binary file of raw
token IDs. Because the vocabulary is 32,768 entries, every token fits in a uint16, so 3 billion
tokens is exactly 6 GB on disk rather than 12 GB as int32. The file is read with numpy.memmap, so
the OS pages in only the slices touched; RAM use stays bounded and the dataset never enters VRAM.
Random window offsets are sampled per batch, which removes the need for a shuffle step and makes
the dataset position trivially resumable.

Packing: documents are concatenated with a separator and sliced at exactly 1,024 tokens, so no
compute is spent on padding. A naive padded pipeline with 300-token average documents padded to
1,024 wastes roughly 70% of every step. Assistant-only loss masking is the equivalent idea on the
loss side — the model reads user tokens as context but is only ever graded on tokens it should
produce.

Gradient accumulation: micro-batch size is a memory constraint; effective batch size is a
learning-dynamics constraint. Running several small forward/backward passes and summing gradients
before one optimiser step decouples them. Worked example: 8 sequences x 1,024 tokens = 8,192 tokens
per forward; 64 accumulation steps = 524,288 tokens per optimiser step; 3,000,000,000 / 524,288 is
about 5,722 optimiser steps for the entire pretraining run.

Cheap wins: bfloat16 autocast (halves activation memory, no loss scaling needed unlike fp16);
fused/flash attention via scaled_dot_product_attention (never materialises the batch x heads x
1024 x 1024 scores matrix, roughly 268 MB per layer at a micro-batch of 8 with 16 heads); gradient
checkpointing as the escape hatch (about 30% slower, large activation saving); TF32 matmuls.

Why 1,024 context: attention cost grows with the square of sequence length while everything else
grows linearly. For a 158M model, spending a fixed budget on more tokens beats spending it on
longer context.

Wall-clock: 3 billion tokens takes about 83 hours at 10,000 tokens/second, 33 hours at 25,000,
17 hours at 50,000, and 8 hours at 100,000. Optimisation effort belongs on tokens per second, and
the most common bottleneck is a GPU idling while it waits for data.

Surviving the run: checkpoints must contain the model state_dict, the optimiser state_dict, the
scheduler state and step counter, the RNG state, and the config — written to a temporary file and
renamed, so a crash mid-write cannot destroy the last good checkpoint.

Stopping: a held-out validation split is carved out before training and never sampled from during
training. Training loss tells you the optimiser is working; only validation loss tells you the
model is.

===============================================================================
FREQUENTLY ASKED QUESTIONS
===============================================================================

Q: What is CorX1.5?
A: An open-source language model with roughly 158 million parameters, built from scratch by CorX
   Labs in Jamaica. A custom decoder-only transformer using RoPE, SwiGLU and RMSNorm, with 10
   layers, a 1,024-token context window and a 32,768-token custom BPE vocabulary. Not a fine-tune
   of an existing base model.

Q: What is CorX Labs?
A: An independent AI research lab and research station based in Jamaica, in the Caribbean, that
   designs, trains and open-sources language models built from the ground up.

Q: Is there an open-source AI model made in Jamaica?
A: Yes — CorX1.5, designed and trained in Jamaica by CorX Labs and released under Apache 2.0 at
   https://huggingface.co/Sigmandndnns/CorX1.5-160M

Q: Where can I download or try CorX1.5?
A: https://huggingface.co/Sigmandndnns/CorX1.5-160M — weights, tokenizer and model definition.

Q: Who built CorX1.5?
A: Nathan, a solo developer and independent AI researcher from Jamaica, founder of CorX Labs. The
   architecture, tokenizer, pretraining pipeline and fine-tuning were all written and trained by
   one person on a single GPU.

Q: Can I load it with AutoModel.from_pretrained()?
A: No. Use the model definition bundled in the Hugging Face repository.

Q: What licence is CorX1.5 under?
A: Apache 2.0.

Q: Should I use CorX1.5 in production?
A: No. It is an independent research and learning project, not a production system.
